5	\label{sec:results-classification}
6	
7	Generation depth proves classifiable across diverse architectures: the 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).

9	We therefore adopt leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+)\,=\,0.694, CI [0.688, 0.700], as the primary metric throughout; it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing.
10	Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).
11	
12	\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
13	Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.764 under 5-fold CV.\footnote{Cross-model chains use the original five-generator subset (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen); Llama and Mistral were added later for single-generator evaluation. Sample-level CV is used because each chain contains multiple generators, making generator-level held-out splits inapplicable. Sample-level splits may introduce within-chain correlation; chain-level (seed-level) validation remains open.}
14	The higher cross-model F1 (vs.\ 0.694 single-generator LOGO) may reflect generator heterogeneity amplifying depth-correlated distributional shifts; generator identity information in mixed chains could partially confound the depth signal.
15	A single-generator transfer analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}) provides evidence against this confound: classifiers trained on one generator transfer to all seven others with mean binary F1\,=\,0.810 (95\% CI [0.796, 0.822]), significantly above chance.
16	Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation yields binary F1\,=\,0.686, consistent with cross-family transfer.
17	A scale effect emerges: Pythia generators achieve the highest binary F1 (0.718--0.724), while larger models show degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633), partly reflecting same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model (cross-reference spread $\leq$0.013; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
18	Preliminary cross-domain evaluation suggests the signal persists with variation, though a domain$\times$temperature interaction exists (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}).
19	An end-to-end QLoRA classifier achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-generator LOGO; $+$11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), which indicates that richer representations capture additional depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; on instruct data, QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91 (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).

23

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base; this is classification F1, distinct from the clustering silhouette of the same value reported in \S\ref{sec:discussion}) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth profiling to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) and closed-source models remain untested; the consistent scale trend (Mistral-7B binary F1\,=\,0.633, lowest among all generators) suggests depth signal may weaken further at frontier scales, potentially approaching the detection floor.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type binary F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730) and rewriting (0.737), with within-prompt-type paraphrastic chains showing weaker signal (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for within-prompt-type continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

Independent-seed validation covers two of eight generators (Pythia-2.8B and Pythia-1B); extending to all generators, particularly Mistral-7B (lowest LOGO F1), would strengthen seed-independence claims.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) at both $t{=}1.0$ and $t{=}0.7$ shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 0.63--0.75 depending on domain and temperature), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: at $t{=}0.7$, Academic domain binary F1 drops to 0.628, suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A temperature ablation across four generators from three families (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows that the method operates reliably within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp across generators). Low-temperature improvement is model-dependent (Pythia/OLMo: $+7$--$9$\,pp; Qwen: $0$--$2$\,pp), indicating that depth profiling assumes standard decoding regimes and that the benefit of conservative temperature varies by model family.
Tokenizer differences across families may contribute to the observed temperature sensitivity pattern; within-family comparisons (two Qwen models showing consistent robustness) support a family-level effect, but controlling for tokenizer requires further study.

Simpler features (character or word n-gram frequencies) were not explored; they may capture complementary surface-level patterns but would not contribute to the location/shape decomposition central to this analysis.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad}, and model collapse is inevitable without fresh human data \cite{curse_of_recursion}, though careful data mixing can mitigate this \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
Self-training and self-play approaches \cite{self_rewarding_lms,spin} also involve iterative self-generation but optimize a training objective; these studies focus on training-loop degradation, whereas our setting studies inference chains.
The distinction extends beyond setting: model collapse erodes distributional tail coverage irreversibly as training progresses \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}. In contrast, the inference-chain drift we observe is fully reversible under fixed parameters, and distributional shape exhibits negligible depth effects (Cohen's $d < 0.10$; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
The drifting/intermediate/near-stationary tri-partition central to our analysis has no analogue in model collapse studies, which track aggregate divergence without separating location from shape components.
Three concurrent works are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss under semantic-preservation constraints that confine depth signal to surface-level lexical decay.
\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that such constraints induce Markovian attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
\citet{attractor_cycles} provide a dynamical-systems analysis of successive paraphrasing, identifying attractor cycles that characterize convergence behavior; our work extends the attractor perspective to non-paraphrastic continuation chains with a feature-level decomposition.
All three study paraphrastic chains; we differ in three respects: (i) non-paraphrastic continuation chains permit richer drift (both semantic and distributional); (ii) handcrafted features enable the DDR decomposition into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary components; and (iii) our tri-partition reveals \emph{what} converges (location) versus what remains stable (shape), while their analyses characterize \emph{that} convergence occurs.
That all three works independently converge on approximately three distinguishable classes reflects different mechanisms reaching the same ceiling: Markovian attractor dynamics in semantic space \cite{markovian_chains}, surface-level lexical decay under paraphrastic constraints \cite{broken_telephone}, and feature-space compression in continuation chains (inter-class KS drops from 0.28 to 0.09 after depth 2; this work).

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features (TTR and hapax ratio) are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship,neal2017surveying}; more sophisticated alternatives exist (MTLD, HD-D \cite{mccarthy2010mtld}; MATTR \cite{covington2010mattr}) but TTR and hapax ratio suffice for depth discrimination.
We push beyond generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the \emph{depth} dimension under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling}.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
\label{sec:related-provenance}

Scalable data curation relies on quality signals \cite{dsir,qurating,ccnet}, and recent work highlights the challenge of detecting training data contamination \cite{oren2024proving,golchin2024time} and maintaining data provenance at scale \cite{longpre2024data}.
Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal characterizing \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source.
Proactive watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns, but watermark strength decays across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, which motivates passive post-hoc methods like ours.
At the feature level, our NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for generation depth classification.

Yet binary detection decisions \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} obscure this structure: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

No existing method provides a feature-level decomposition of depth signal in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When the output of a language model is fed back as input to another (or the same) model, the resulting generation chain defines a discrete dynamical system over text distributions.
How do the distributional properties of generated text evolve across successive steps of this recursion?
Understanding this evolution is fundamental to characterizing how language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with implications for model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} and data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} as model outputs increasingly re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} (an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}).
Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by coarse ordinal depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, but none decompose the drift into structurally distinct components; our work addresses this gap in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure the distributional dynamics of recursive generation; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation producing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution; one hypothesis is that the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.

Because drifting features capture the progressive location shift while stationary features provide a stable reference, combining them yields a classifier that generalizes across generators: binary F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and 0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, outperforming individual detection baselines by 6--11\,pp at 2.4$\times$ lower computational cost.

Our contributions are threefold:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary detection to ordinal depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and construct an evaluation suite of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We decompose inference-chain drift into structurally distinct components: central-tendency features drift monotonically ($d = 0.76$--$1.17$) while shape features remain an order of magnitude more stable ($d < 0.10$), a decomposition absent from existing attractor dynamics and model collapse analyses. A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this \emph{differential depth response} achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains.
    \item Comprehensive evaluation reveals that DDR is temperature-robust (${\leq}1$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.9]$), prompt-type modulated (continuation $>$ elaboration), and absent in instruction-tuned models; equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$) confirms no downstream quality degradation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
\end{enumerate}

5	This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

9	Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow$ mismatch: F1 from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
10	These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).
11	
12	DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
13	Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean log-probability systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow$ mismatch: F1 from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though richer representations recover substantially more signal (QLoRA F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction-tuned models show attenuated fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base), confirming that alignment procedures compress the feature margins DDR exploits.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift.

\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).

Per-feature convergence trajectories confirm this ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:convergence}); the DDR partition hierarchy is preserved across temperatures despite absolute effect-size compression (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).
